summary: This unit teaches you to coordinate the materials for a fabrication job as a team leader: working out everything the job needs from the drawings, planning when each item must arrive, receiving, storing and handling it safely, keeping material traceability on coded jobs, issuing materials to the welders and tracking what is used, and dealing with shortages, offcuts, surplus and scrap. You will also learn to work with purchasing, stores, the drawing office and the inspector, and to report the materials position to your manager.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It is about **coordinating materials**: making sure that the steel, consumables, gases, paint and bought-in parts for a job are there when the welders need them, in the right amount and condition, and that their use is tracked from the store to the finished item.

A welding team that stops to search for plate, waits for gas, or re-cuts a frame because the wrong angle was issued is losing money every minute. So is a yard full of steel delivered weeks early and left to rust. The team leader who coordinates materials well keeps the work flowing and the cost under control.

**Who it is for:** Level 3 welders, fitters and team leaders who plan and run fabrication jobs, and storekeepers who support them. The unit links closely with purchasing (buying the materials) and housekeeping (keeping the store and bays in order); here the focus is on planning, flow, traceability and control.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Work out what the job needs
Prepare a bill of materials from the approved drawings, plan cutting from standard lengths and sheets, estimate consumables, and check the stock first.
Build a materials schedule from the programme and the suppliers' lead times, with staged deliveries.
Check deliveries against the order and certificates, and store each material so it stays in good condition and is easy to find.
Work out masses, choose the right lifting equipment and methods, and load trucks safely.
On coded jobs, link every piece to its mill certificate by heat number, from delivery to the finished item.
Issue against the bill of materials, kit parts by assembly, book every issue to a job, keep bin cards right and investigate differences.
Compare what was used with the estimate, measure scrap and yield, and act to reduce waste.
Deal with shortages, surplus and scrap
Find shortages early, never substitute without approval, mark and reuse offcuts, and sort scrap.
Keep purchasing, stores, the drawing office, the inspector and the manager informed, and send a short weekly materials report.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on requirements, scheduling, traceability, storage, consumables, handling, issuing, stock control, monitoring use, offcuts, shortages, hazardous materials, liaison and reporting. Several questions are short calculations.

A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as bill of materials, traceability, FIFO, just in time, bin card, stocktake, issue note, offcuts and SDS, and calculations of mass, quantities and percentages) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Two group practicals:** a bill of materials, cutting plan, nesting sketch and materials schedule for a fabricated stand, with a store check against the bin cards; and receiving, marking, storing and issuing materials for a coded job while keeping traceability.

blocks.note: Most calculation marks are lost by not rounding up. You cannot order 6.4 lengths, 3.5 spools or 5.3 cylinders: always round **up** to the next whole length, spool or cylinder.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: To **coordinate materials** means making sure the right materials are in the right place, in the right amount and condition, at the right time, and that their use is tracked and costed. A useful check is the five rights:

head: Right ...
What it means
What goes wrong without it
rows: The grade, size and finish on the drawing, with certificates where the job needs them
Wrong grade welded in; rework; failed inspection
Enough for the job, with a sensible allowance, but not a yard full of surplus
Work stops; or cash and space tied up
Dry, clean, straight, undamaged, in date
At the bay or site where it will be used, or in its marked store location
Time lost searching and double handling
Arriving just before it is needed, with a margin for delays
Welders idle; or steel rusting for weeks

blocks.h: The flow of materials through a job

flow: Requirements: the bill of materials from the approved drawings
Schedule: when each item must be in the shop, from the programme and lead times
Order: requisitions to purchasing, with full specifications and dates
Receive: check quantity, size, grade, condition and certificates
Store: in the right place and condition, labelled with the job number
Issue: kits and consumables against the job, recorded
Monitor: compare what is used with the estimate
Close out: book back surplus, mark and rack offcuts, sort and sell scrap, report

head: Who
What you need from them
What they need from you
rows: Approved drawings, the bill of materials, every new revision
Questions, shortages found, offcuts already in stock
Order and delivery confirmations, warnings of late deliveries
Requisitions with full specifications and the date needed; any change to the plan
Stock levels, receipts, issues, stocktake results
The materials schedule, job numbers, returns and offcuts booked back
What they need and when; problems with materials
Kits and consumables on time; cutting lists; clear instructions
A weekly materials report; usage against the estimate
A fair share of the lifting equipment
A daily lifting schedule agreed in advance

blocks.note: When a plan changes (a job brought forward, a drawing revised, a delivery late), tell everyone affected at once, in writing. Stores and purchasing need to know first, because their orders and deliveries are planned around the old dates.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Working out what the job needs

blocks.p: The **bill of materials (BOM)** lists every material and bought-in part needed to make an item, with sizes and quantities. Prepare it from the **approved drawings at their latest revision**, never from memory of a similar job or from whatever steel is lying in the yard.

head: Mark
Description
Grade
Length or size
No. off
Remarks
rows: Check the date on the tin

blocks.p: Add the consumables, gases, paint, bolts and fixings: they are as much part of the job as the steel, and a missing box of bolts can hold up erection as surely as missing steel.
Sections come in standard lengths, often 6 m. A **cutting list** plans which pieces come out of each length so that little is left over. Plan different pieces of the same section together:

head: Needed: 12 pieces of 1.8 m and 12 of 1.1 m from 6 m lengths
Lengths needed
rows: Cut separately: 3 × 1.8 m per length (5.4 m) needs 4 lengths; 5 × 1.1 m per length (5.5 m) needs 12 ÷ 5 = 2.4, so 3 lengths
Cut together: 1.8 + 1.8 + 1.1 + 1.1 = 5.8 m per length, so 6 lengths give all 24 pieces

ul: Each saw cut turns a little steel into swarf: the width of the blade or disc, often a few millimetres. Allow for it, and for squaring up rough ends, when a piece only just fits.
Check the total too: 12 × 1.8 + 12 × 1.1 = 34.8 m, and 34.8 ÷ 6 = 5.8, so no plan can use fewer than 6 lengths.

blocks.p: Plate parts are **nested** (fitted closely together) on standard sheets to waste as little as possible. The **yield** is the percentage of the sheet that ends up as parts:

**Yield = area of parts ÷ area of sheet × 100.** Example: a 2400 × 1200 mm sheet is 2.4 × 1.2 = 2.88 m². Parts totalling 2.16 m² give 2.16 ÷ 2.88 × 100 = 75%. The other 25% is skeleton and offcut: on a 10 mm sheet weighing 2.88 × 0.010 × 7850 = 226 kg, that is about 56.5 kg.

ul: Steel has a density of about **7850 kg/m³**.
Plate mass = length × width × thickness (all in metres) × 7850. A 1.2 m × 2.4 m × 12 mm plate: 1.2 × 2.4 × 0.012 = 0.03456 m³ × 7850 ≈ 271 kg.
Section mass = mass per metre (from the supplier's table) × length. Ten 6 m lengths at 12 kg/m: 10 × 6 × 12 = 720 kg.
1 tonne = 1000 kg.

**Welding wire and electrodes:** estimate from the weld lengths and sizes, using the estimator's figures or the maker's tables. Round up to whole spools or packets: 52 kg of wire on 15 kg spools is 3.47, so issue 4 spools.
**Gas:** from how long a cylinder lasts on similar work. If one cylinder lasts about 3 working days and the welding takes 16 days, 16 ÷ 3 = 5.3, so plan 6 cylinders.
**Paint:** area to be painted ÷ the coverage on the data sheet (m² per litre at the specified thickness), plus an allowance for losses. 46 m² at 8 m² per litre is 5.75 litres before losses.
**Grinding and cutting discs, gloves and other small items:** from past jobs of the same size.
Add a sensible allowance for offcuts and mistakes, and for spare bolts (for example 10%, rounded up to whole bolts), as the estimator or the shop's practice says.
Before anything is ordered, check the store and the offcut rack. Marked offcuts of the right grade and size can save buying a whole new length.
Check that stock you plan to use is not already promised to another job.
Mark on the BOM what is in stock and what must be ordered.

blocks.p: A **materials schedule** shows when each item must be in the shop, matched to the job programme. Cutting starts with the plate and main sections; bolts and fittings are needed at assembly; paint only near the end.
**Latest order date = date needed − lead time − time for receiving checks** (and any margin you choose). For the plate: 18 − 7 − 2 = day 9.

blocks.h: Why not bring everything in on day one?

ul: Space: a small yard fills up, blocks walkways and makes every lift harder.
Cash: money is tied up in steel that will not be used for weeks.
Condition: steel left out rusts; paint and consumables age.
Loss: more stock lying about means more damage, mix-ups and theft.

blocks.p: **Just in time (JIT)** means materials arrive just before they are needed, so little stock is held. It saves space and cash, but it needs reliable suppliers. For long-lead or imported items, or in the hurricane season, keep a margin or a small buffer stock, because one late ship can stop the job.

ul: Ask for deliveries in stages, timed to the cutting and assembly plan, when the yard is small or the job is long.
Agree a delivery window, where the truck will park and unload, and which crane or forklift will be free.
Avoid deliveries at times when the lifting equipment is booked for other work.

flow: Check the delivery note against the purchase order and the BOM: items, sizes, grades, quantities
Check the condition: bends, rust, damaged coatings, wet or torn packs
On coded jobs, check every heat number against a mill certificate showing the right grade
Write any shortage or damage on the delivery note before signing it
Record the receipt on the goods received note and the bin cards
Label job materials with the job number and put them in their store location
Quarantine rejected items, labelled, and report them to purchasing

blocks.note: A delivery that matches no order or schedule is held to one side, unused, until purchasing has checked it. It may belong to another job, another customer, or be a supplier's mistake.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Material
How to store it
Why
rows: On racks or timber bearers, off the ground, sorted by size and grade and labelled
Never stood upright against a wall or post
Stays dry and straight; easy to find; cannot topple onto someone
In a plate rack on edge, or flat on bearers with packing between sheets
So it can be reached with a plate clamp
On their own racks, never touching carbon steel
Protective film left on until fabrication
Away from carbon steel grinding and cutting
Carbon steel dust and contact leave rust spots on stainless and contaminate aluminium
Stacked with spacers so air can pass between pieces, and kept off wet ground
Galvanising stacked tight and wet grows white rust (wet storage stain)
In a dry store, in sealed packs
Opened low-hydrogen electrodes in the holding oven
MIG wire in its sealed bag until it goes on the machine
Moisture causes porosity and hydrogen cracking
Upright, chained, capped, ventilated and shaded; oxygen apart from fuel gases; full apart from empty
In a ventilated store away from hot work, with the safety data sheet (SDS) on file

blocks.p: Issue the oldest stock first: **first in, first out (FIFO)**. New deliveries go behind or under the older stock. This matters most for items with a shelf life, such as paint, primer, sealants and some fluxes, but it also stops steel lying in the rack until it rusts.

ul: Low-hydrogen electrodes left out overnight in a humid shop pick up moisture. Re-dry them exactly as the maker says, or set them aside; never use them "before they get damper".
Issue them in small amounts, in a heated quiver (portable rod oven), and take unused ones back to the holding oven at the end of the shift.
Keep MIG wire sealed until it is loaded, and cover a spool left on a machine overnight.

blocks.p: Rain and humid sea air rust bare steel and spoil consumables. Cover steel delivered in the rainy months, keep it off the ground on bearers so water drains away, and protect galvanised and painted work from standing water.

blocks.note: Jamaica's wettest months are usually around May–June and September–November, and the hurricane season runs from 1 June to 30 November. When a storm warning is issued, bring loose sheets, offcuts and small sections indoors or tie them down: in a hurricane they become flying missiles. Check that racks and cylinder chains are secure and that yard drains are clear.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Keep valuable items such as welding cable, brass regulators, power tools and stainless offcuts in a locked store or site container.
Control the keys: a short list of named holders.
Sign items in and out, and count them at set times.
Mark tools and equipment with the company's name or number.

blocks.note: Steel for one job stacked unlabelled in the general rack will be used on other jobs. Label it with the job number on arrival, and keep certified steel apart from general stock.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Before anything is moved, work out roughly what it weighs. A 10 mm plate only 1.5 m × 1.0 m weighs about 118 kg; a bundle of channel can weigh close to a tonne. Guidance figures for one person lifting by hand are low, around 25 kg held close to the body at waist height, and much less when reaching, twisting or lifting from the floor. Plate and bundles are moved with lifting equipment, not by hand.

head: Load
Equipment
Points to watch
rows: Crane or hoist with a plate clamp of the right type, or a vacuum lifter
Clamp's safe working load (SWL) and jaw range suit the plate
Never drag plate off a rack onto the floor
Crane with two slings, or a lifting beam, near each end
Tag lines to steady and turn it
Within the truck's rating; pallet sound
Two or more people, with one calling the lift
Lift and set down together; watch fingers between lengths
Clean soft (synthetic) slings, or clamps kept for these metals
Chains and dirty clamps scratch the finish and leave carbon steel on it

ul: Every sling, shackle, clamp and lifting beam is marked with its **safe working load (SWL)** and has a current inspection tag or colour code. Damaged or untagged gear is not used.
The SWL of each item must be more than the share of the load it will carry.
Only trained people operate cranes and forklifts, with one trained person giving signals.
Plan the route, clear it, and keep everyone out from under the load and out of the forklift's path.
Nobody rides on a load or on the forks.

blocks.p: With a two-leg sling, the wider the angle between the legs, the more load each leg carries. At a wide enough angle each leg carries the whole weight of the load.

head: Angle between the two legs
Load in each leg (as a share of the total)
For a 900 kg bundle

blocks.note: Keep the angle between sling legs at 90° or less unless the sling's chart allows more. Long slings give a smaller angle; short slings on a wide load give a dangerously large one.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: When two teams need the only crane at the same time, agree a **lifting schedule** for the day at the start of the shift, with times for each team, based on the job priorities. First come, first served leads to arguments, rushed lifts and people lifting by hand instead.

ul: Load on timber bearers, in the order the parts will be unloaded and erected, so the first parts needed come off first.
Strap the load down so it cannot slide or roll, with edge protectors where straps cross painted or galvanised edges.
Mark any part that overhangs the end of the truck with a red flag or marker, and keep within the road rules for overhang and width.
Send a packing list with the piece marks, and check the load against it before the truck leaves.

blocks.note: Wear gloves, safety boots and a hard hat when handling steel. Keep hands out of pinch points between lengths and between the load and the rack.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Traceability** means being able to follow any piece of steel in a finished job back to its mill certificate and supplier. On jobs built to a code (pressure pipe, structural steel, tanks) it proves that each part is made of the certified material. If a problem is found later, it also shows which other parts came from the same heat.

Each **heat** (one melt) of steel has a **heat number**, stamped or painted on every length and plate, and a **mill certificate** giving its chemical analysis and test results. Traceability is the chain that links the two at every step.

flow: On receipt, check that every heat number matches a certificate showing the right grade; file the certificates in the job file
Store certified steel apart from general stock, labelled with the job number
Before cutting, transfer the heat number and job number to every piece that will be cut off, including offcuts going back to the rack
Keep a cutting record that lists each part mark against its heat number
Record the batch numbers of the welding consumables used
Have the inspector check the marks at the hold points, before welding or paint hides them
At the end, the job file links every part to its heat number and certificate

ul: Use a paint marker, or a low-stress (round-nosed) stamp where the procedure allows stamping. Sharp hard stamps can start cracks in some materials, and some codes forbid them.
Put the marks where they will still be seen after fabrication, or note the part mark on the cutting record before the mark is lost.

head: Problem
What to do
rows: A heat number is not on any certificate, or the certificate shows the wrong grade
Hold the steel; report to purchasing and the inspector; do not use it until the right certificate is received
An offcut has lost its marks
Quarantine it; it may be used on coded work only if its source can be proved from the cutting record and the inspector agrees; otherwise use it only on uncoded work
Marks were ground off or painted over during fabrication
Stop; re-establish the marks from the cutting record with the inspector before the work goes further
A consumable batch is found faulty
Use the batch records to find every weld made with it

blocks.note: Never "fix" traceability by painting a heat number onto a piece because it looks like the others. A wrong mark is worse than no mark: it makes the record false.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Issue materials against the BOM and cutting list, not just because someone asks.

**Kitting:** for each assembly, the store puts together the cut parts, bolts and consumables in a tray or stillage marked with the job and assembly numbers, so welders do not stop to search for parts.
Record every issue on an **issue note**, so the job's real material cost is known.
Update the bin cards at the time of issue, not at the end of the week.
Book unused materials and full lengths back to the store against the job at the end of each day or job.

head: Issue note (example)
Entry
rows: Kit 3: parts L3-1 to L3-12; 24 × M16 bolts; 2 packets 3.2 mm E7018

blocks.p: A **bin card** is kept with each stock item and shows what came in, what went out and the balance. It must agree with the stock on the shelf.

ul: Gas, electrodes, wire and discs are used on every job, so set a reorder point and reorder when the stock reaches it.
**Reorder point = daily use × lead time (days) + safety stock.** Using 3 boxes a day, with a 5-day lead time and 6 boxes safety stock: 3 × 5 + 6 = 21 boxes.
**Days of stock left = stock ÷ daily use.** 21 boxes at 3 a day last 7 days.
**Average monthly use** = total over the months ÷ number of months: 48 + 55 + 41 = 144; 144 ÷ 3 = 48 a month.

blocks.p: A **stocktake** is a count of every item in the store, compared with the records. When the count and the bin card disagree:

flow: Count again, carefully, with a second person
Look for the cause: an issue or receipt not recorded, items in the wrong place, damage, a counting error or theft
Correct the record, with the reason, signed by the person allowed to approve it
Report losses to the manager and tighten the control that failed

blocks.p: **Difference as a percentage of the recorded stock = difference ÷ recorded × 100.** Records 60, count 54: 6 ÷ 60 × 100 = 10% missing.

sections.title: Monitoring use, shortages, surplus and reporting

ul: **Over the estimate (%) = (used − estimated) ÷ estimated × 100.** Estimated 3 200 kg, used 3 360 kg: 160 ÷ 3 200 × 100 = 5% over.
**Scrap (%) = (issued − in the finished work) ÷ issued × 100.** Issued 2 500 kg, finished items contain 2 300 kg: 200 ÷ 2 500 × 100 = 8%.
Compare every job with its estimate, find the reasons for differences, and pass the figures to the estimator so the next estimate is better.

head: Common cause of extra use
What the team leader can do
rows: Poor cutting plans and loose nesting
Plan cuts and nests before cutting; check yield
New lengths cut while good offcuts sit in the rack
Check the offcut rack first; part-used sheets and offcuts used before new stock
Measure twice, check the first part against the drawing, correct cutting settings, coach the person
Rework after poor welds or fit-up
Find the cause and correct it; record the cost
Issue measured amounts; keep them dry; use electrodes down to a short stub

flow: Find shortages early, by checking the schedule against stock and deliveries every week
Check the facts: how much is needed, what is in stock, usable offcuts, stock held for other jobs
Tell purchasing at once and look for the earliest delivery from approved suppliers
Re-plan the work so the team can carry on with parts that do not need the missing item
Tell the manager, and the client if the date may slip
Afterwards, find out why the shortage was not seen sooner

blocks.note: Never change the grade, thickness or size of a material without the written approval of the engineer or supervisor, even if the substitute is thicker or stronger. A change can affect the strength, the weight, the fit, the welding procedure and the certificates the client expects.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Offcuts** worth keeping are marked with their size and grade (and heat number on coded work) and stored on the offcut rack.
Full lengths, sheets and unopened consumables left at the end of a job are checked and booked back into stock against the job.
Material bought specially for a client and charged to them may belong to the client: check the contract and offer it to them.
Slow-moving stock that no job has used for a long time is offered to other jobs or sold, rather than kept for ever.
Scrap is sorted into carbon steel, stainless steel and aluminium, kept apart from rubbish, and sold for recycling.

blocks.p: Plan the dispatch of finished parts with the site team: load them in erection order, with a packing list showing every piece mark, coatings protected, and deliveries staged to suit the space on site and the crane.

head: Section of the report
What it shows
rows: Due this week, arrived, late (with the new date) or rejected
Expected in the next two weeks, and the action being taken
Common items near their reorder point
Used so far against the estimate; stocktake differences; waste
Items the manager must decide, such as approving a substitute or overtime

blocks.p: Keep it short, written and in the same format each week. Problems seen early can still be fixed; the manager can plan labour and promise dates with confidence, and costs are controlled before they run away.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section.

ul: I can explain what coordinating materials means and name the people a team leader must work with.
I can prepare a bill of materials from approved drawings, including consumables, bolts and paint.
I can plan cuts from standard lengths and nest plate parts, and work out the number of lengths and the yield.
I can work out the mass of plate and sections, and estimate wire, gas and paint, rounding up to whole units.
I can build a materials schedule and work out the latest order date from the lead time.
I can explain the benefits and risks of staged deliveries and just in time.
I can receive a delivery and check it against the order, the BOM and the certificates.
I can store sections, plate, stainless, galvanised steel, consumables, cylinders and paint correctly, and issue stock first in, first out.
I can prepare the yard for heavy rain and storms, and keep materials secure.
I can choose safe handling methods and lifting gear, and explain how the sling angle changes the load in each leg.
I can keep traceability by heat number from delivery to the finished item, and deal with traceability problems.
I can issue kits and consumables against a job with an issue note, keep bin cards right and set reorder points.
I can carry out a stocktake and deal with differences.
I can compare use with the estimate, measure scrap, and act to reduce waste.
I can deal with a shortage without making an unapproved substitution.
I can deal with offcuts, surplus, client-owned material and scrap at the end of a job.
I can plan the dispatch of parts to site and write a weekly materials report.

terms: Bill of materials (BOM)
A list of every material and bought-in part needed to make an item, with sizes and quantities
Bin card
A card kept with a stock item showing what came in, what went out and the balance
Cutting list
A plan of which pieces are cut from each standard length
FIFO
First in, first out: the oldest stock is issued first
Heat number
The number identifying one melt of steel, marked on the steel and on its mill certificate
Holding oven
A heated cabinet that keeps opened low-hydrogen electrodes dry
Issue note
The record of materials handed out to a job: job number, item, quantity and signatures
Just in time (JIT)
Materials arrive just before they are needed, so little stock is held
Kitting
Putting all the parts and consumables for one assembly together, marked, before work starts
Lead time
The time between placing an order and receiving the goods
Materials schedule
A plan showing when each item must be in the shop
Mill certificate
The steel maker's record of the analysis and test results for one heat
Nesting
Fitting plate parts closely together on a sheet to reduce waste
Offcut
A short piece left over after cutting, marked and kept for later use
Packing list
A list of the pieces in a load or crate, with their marks
Reorder point
The stock level at which a new order is placed
SDS
Safety data sheet: the maker's sheet on a product's hazards, storage and first aid
Stocktake
Counting every item in the store and comparing the count with the records
SWL
Safe working load: the most a piece of lifting gear may carry
Tag line
A rope tied to a load to steady and guide it during a lift
Traceability
Being able to follow each piece in a job back to its certificate and supplier
Yield
The percentage of a sheet or length that ends up as parts

c1.title: Water-tank stands in St Ann's Bay
c1.text: Delroy Ricketts is team leader at a fabrication shop in St Ann's Bay, St Ann, coordinating materials for four water-tank stands for a primary school. From the approved drawings, the stands need 16 legs of 2.4 m and 32 braces of 1.1 m, all in 75 × 75 × 6 mm angle, which comes in 6 m lengths. The offcut rack holds five pieces of the same angle and grade, each 2.6 m long and properly marked. Delroy sent his bill of materials to purchasing on Monday. On Tuesday the drawing office issued revision C of the drawing, which changes the base plates from 6 mm to 10 mm. Purchasing plans to place the order on Wednesday.

c2.title: Plate parts and an overrun in Black River
c2.text: Annmarie Douglas plans materials at a steel shop in Black River, St Elizabeth. Gusset and base plates for a warehouse frame are nested on sheets of 10 mm plate, 1500 × 3000 mm. On one sheet the parts total 3.15 m². The estimate for the job's steel was 1 800 kg; the job has used 1 890 kg, and Annmarie finds that two frames had to be cut twice after marking-out errors. A welder now asks for a new sheet to cut more gussets, although a part-used sheet of the same grade and thickness is on the rack.

c3.title: Pipe spools to a code in Ewarton
c3.text: Garfield Thompson coordinates materials at a shop in Ewarton, St Catherine, that is making pipe spools to a code for an industrial plant. The pipe arrived with a heat number painted on each length, and the mill certificates are in the job file. A welder has cut one length in two and put a 1.1 m offcut, with no marks on it, back in the general pipe rack. The welders draw E7018 electrodes from the store each morning. The paint shop has asked to prime the finished spools before the inspector has seen them, to save a day.

c4.title: Lifting and loading in Highgate
c4.text: Nickoy Bennett is yard foreman at a fabrication shop in Highgate, St Mary. A bundle of 10 lengths of 6 m channel, which the supplier's table lists at 15 kg per metre, must go by overhead crane to the saw, using the yard's two-leg chain sling. Next, polished stainless sheets must be lifted to the bench, and the only slings to hand are the chain slings used every day on rusty carbon steel. In the afternoon, finished frames will be loaded on a flatbed truck for a site in Hope Bay, Portland; the longest frames will overhang the back of the truck by about 1.5 m.

c5.title: The store in Albert Town
c5.text: Mrs Paulette Bryan keeps the store at a fabrication shop in Albert Town, Trelawny. The shop uses about 2.5 spools of MIG wire each working day; the supplier delivers 4 working days after an order, and the shop keeps a safety stock of 5 spools. A job for a hotel has just finished: six sheets of 316 stainless steel bought specially for it, and charged to the client, are left over, and the welders have brought back three full lengths of RHS. A supplier has offered, at the same price, a stronger grade of plate than the A36 on the drawings for the next job. A hurricane warning has just been issued for Trelawny.

questions.q: Planning the cuts for the legs and braces together, and ignoring saw cuts, what is the fewest number of new 6 m lengths needed if no offcuts are used?
o: 15 lengths
12 lengths
16 lengths
13 lengths
questions.why: Two legs and a brace (2.4 + 2.4 + 1.1 = 5.9 m) come from each of 8 lengths, giving all 16 legs and 8 braces. The other 24 braces fit five to a length (5.5 m), needing 5 more: 13 in all. Cutting legs and braces separately needs 8 + 7 = 15.

questions.q: How should Delroy use the five 2.6 m offcuts?
o: Leave them, as new lengths are always better for a client's job
Check them, use them for five legs, and order less new angle
Cut them into braces, as legs must come from new lengths
Send them for scrap now, since they are only offcuts
questions.why: Marked offcuts of the right grade and size are stock. If they are sound, each 2.6 m piece gives one 2.4 m leg, so five fewer legs come from new lengths and the order can be cut. Checking stock first is part of every BOM.

questions.q: What should Delroy do about revision C?
o: Update the BOM and warn purchasing before Wednesday
Wait until the steel arrives, then order the 10 mm plate
Nothing: base plates are too small to matter to the order
Ask the welders to double up 6 mm plates to make 12 mm
questions.why: Purchasing is about to order from an out-of-date list. Updating the BOM to the latest approved revision and telling purchasing at once, in writing, stops the wrong plate being bought and the job being held up later.

questions.q: About how much of each 10 mm sheet, by mass, is left over as skeleton and offcuts?
o: About 106 kg
About 247 kg
About 35 kg
About 1 060 kg
questions.why: The sheet weighs 1.5 × 3.0 × 0.010 × 7850 ≈ 353 kg. The parts use 3.15 ÷ 4.5 = 70% of it, so 30% is left: 0.30 × 353 ≈ 106 kg. 247 kg is the mass of the parts themselves.

questions.q: What should Annmarie do about the job's steel use?
o: Nothing, since every job uses some extra steel
Report the 5% overrun and deal with its cause
Order 5% less steel for the next job to make up for it
Charge the extra steel to the two welders who made the errors
questions.why: The job is (1 890 − 1 800) ÷ 1 800 × 100 = 5% over. Finding and reporting the cause lets the team prevent it (checking the first part against the drawing, measuring twice, coaching) and helps the estimator price the next job.

questions.q: What should happen about the welder's request for a new sheet?
o: Use the part-used sheet first, if it is the right grade and size
Give him the new sheet, as part-used sheets are only for practice
Give him the new sheet and send the part-used one for scrap
Ask him to cut the gussets from any thicker plate in the rack
questions.why: Part-used sheets and offcuts of the right grade and thickness are used before new stock, which raises the yield and lowers the job's cost. Cutting from a different thickness would need the engineer's approval.

questions.q: What should happen to the unmarked 1.1 m offcut?
o: Paint on the heat number of the nearest length in the rack
Use it on the spools, as it obviously came from the job's pipe
Hold it apart unless its source can be proved
Leave it in the general rack for any job that needs a short piece
questions.why: Without its heat number the offcut cannot be traced to a certificate. It is held apart; if the cutting record and the inspector can prove which length it came from, it can be re-marked, otherwise it is used only on uncoded work.

questions.q: Why should the inspector see the spools before the paint shop primes them?
o: Primer will not stick to steel that has not been inspected
The inspector needs to choose the colour of the primer
Paint would hide the marks and welds to be checked
Inspected steel is lighter to carry to the paint shop
questions.why: The inspection is a hold point: the marks and welds must be checked while they can still be seen. Saving a day by priming first could cost far more if the spools have to be stripped or are rejected.

questions.q: Why should the store record the batch number of the E7018 issued for the spools?
o: So the welds made from a faulty batch can be found later
So the supplier can be paid for each packet as it is used
So the welders can choose their favourite batch next time
So the electrodes need not be kept in the holding oven
questions.why: On coded work, consumables are traceable too. If a batch is later found to be faulty, the records show exactly which welds were made with it, so only those need to be checked or repaired.

questions.q: How should the E7018 be issued to the welders each morning?
o: Small amounts in a heated quiver, unused ones returned
A full day's tin to each welder, left open on the bench
A week's supply at a time, to save trips to the store
Whatever each welder asks for, kept in his toolbox
questions.why: Low-hydrogen electrodes pick up moisture quickly in humid air, which causes porosity and hydrogen cracking. Small issues in a heated quiver, and returning unused rods to the holding oven at the end of the shift, keep them dry.

questions.q: What is the mass of the bundle of channel?
o: 90 kg
900 kg
150 kg
questions.why: Mass = number of lengths × length × mass per metre = 10 × 6 m × 15 kg/m = 900 kg. Knowing it lets Nickoy check the crane, the sling and the hooks are rated for the load.

questions.q: Nickoy's sling legs are short, so they will spread wide over the bundle. Why does this matter?
o: A wide angle makes the bundle swing less as it travels
The angle makes no difference to the load in the legs
The wider the angle, the more load each leg carries
Short legs reduce the total mass the crane must lift
questions.why: At 0° each leg carries half the load, but at 120° each carries the whole 900 kg. Longer slings or a lifting beam keep the angle at 90° or less, unless the sling's chart allows more.

questions.q: How should the polished stainless sheets be lifted?
o: With the chain slings, wiped with an oily rag first
With clean soft slings or a clamp kept for stainless
With the chain slings, then polish out any marks after
By hand, two welders to each sheet, whatever its size
questions.why: Chains used on rusty carbon steel scratch the finish and leave carbon steel particles that later show as rust spots. Clean synthetic slings, or clamps kept only for stainless, protect the sheet.

questions.q: How should the overhanging frames be dealt with on the truck?
o: Ask the driver to go slowly, so no marking is needed
Tie the frames to the truck with welding cable
Put the longest frames on top, loose, for easy unloading
Strap them down and mark the overhang with a red flag
questions.why: A load must be secured so it cannot slide, and an overhang must be clearly marked so other drivers can see it, within the road rules for overhang. Edge protectors stop the straps damaging the coating.

questions.q: At what stock level should Mrs Bryan reorder MIG wire?
o: 10 spools
15 spools
20 spools
12 spools
questions.why: Reorder point = daily use × lead time + safety stock = 2.5 × 4 + 5 = 15 spools. Ordering at 15 leaves 10 spools for the 4 days of waiting and keeps the 5-spool safety stock for delays or a busy week.

questions.q: What should be done with the six leftover sheets of 316 stainless?
o: Put them into general stock for the next stainless job
Sell them to a scrap dealer, as the job is finished
Check the contract and offer them to the client
Cut them up for practice pieces in the training bay
questions.why: Material bought specially for a client and charged to them may belong to the client. The contract says who owns surplus; if it is the client's, it is offered to them or credited, not used on another job.

questions.q: Why should the three full lengths of RHS be booked back to the store against the hotel job?
o: So the welders who returned them can be paid a bonus
So the RHS can be thrown out at the next stocktake
So the supplier will collect them and refund the shop
So job cost and stock records are right
questions.why: If returns are not booked back, the hotel job is charged for steel it did not use, and the store holds steel its records do not show. Both make future estimates and stock counts wrong.

questions.q: What should be done about the supplier's offer of a stronger plate?
o: Accept it, as stronger steel can only make the job better
Accept it, but tell the welders to use more current
Refuse it, as the drawings can never be changed
Refer it to the engineer for written approval first
questions.why: A different grade can weld differently, need a different procedure and need different certificates, even if it is stronger. Only the engineer can approve the change, in writing, before the plate is ordered.

questions.q: With the hurricane warning, what should be done with the loose sheets and offcuts in the yard?
o: Leave them, as steel is too heavy to be moved by wind
Stack them higher so they take up less room
Move them indoors or tie them down securely
Cover them with loose plastic sheeting only
questions.why: Hurricane winds can lift sheets and small pieces and throw them like missiles. Bring them in or tie them down, secure the racks and cylinders, and clear the yard drains before the storm.

questions.q: Steel delivered for Job 418 has been stacked in the general rack with no labels. What is the main risk?
o: It will rust faster than steel that is labelled
The crane cannot lift steel that has no label
The supplier will not accept it back if it is unlabelled
It may be used on other jobs, leaving Job 418 short
questions.why: Unlabelled job steel looks like general stock, so other teams take it and Job 418 runs short at the worst moment. Labelling with the job number on receipt, and keeping job and certified steel apart, prevents this.
